passages.happening:
“Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD: ‘I will sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted. The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea’” (verse 1).

“The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father’s God, and I will exalt Him. The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is His name” (verses 2-3).

The enemy boasted, “I will pursue, I will overtake. I will divide the spoils” (verse 9). “But You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters” (verse 10).

“Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 14 told the crossing in prose. Chapter 15 answers it in song. It is the first hymn in the Bible.

Hebrew poetry is built from pairs of lines. The second line echoes, sharpens or completes the first: ‘Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power; Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy’ (verse 6).

The first part of the song looks back at the sea. Three pictures describe the enemy's fall: they sank ‘like a stone’, they were consumed ‘like stubble’, they sank ‘like lead’.

Listen to the enemy's boast in verse 9. It is six short bursts, and every one is about himself: I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide, I will gorge, I will draw, my hand will destroy. God's answer is one line. He simply breathed.

‘Who among the gods is like You?’ Neighboring peoples told stories of storm gods who fought the sea and then built a palace on a mountain. This song tells of the LORD using the sea as his weapon, not fighting it as a rival. The gods of Egypt are no match for him.

Many scholars, among them Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman, have argued from its language that this is one of the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible. Others date it later.
passages.later:
Verse 2 is repeated almost word for word later in the Bible: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation” (Psalm 118:14), and “For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation” (Isaiah 12:2). The song of the exodus became Israel's way of praising God for every later rescue.

At the end of the Bible, those who have overcome stand beside a sea “and they sang the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).
passages.hard:
What should we make of praising God as ‘a warrior’ and celebrating the drowning of an army? ‘The LORD is a warrior’ can sound strange to modern ears.

It helps to see what the song does and does not celebrate. Israel did not fight. The song gives the victory entirely to God, and it praises him for rescuing slaves from the army sent to drag them back. In the ancient world, to call a god a warrior meant he could protect and rescue his people. The song claims that power for the LORD alone.

The Bible elsewhere shows restraint about rejoicing when enemies fall: “Do not gloat when your enemy falls” (Proverbs 24:17). Later Jewish tradition kept a story of God rebuking the angels who wanted to sing while the Egyptians drowned.

Readers differ on how to weigh the violence of passages like this. Some see just judgment on oppression, told in the language of its time. Others stress that the Bible's own story moves toward a warrior who wins by suffering rather than by the sword: the Lion of Judah who turns out to be “a Lamb who appeared to have been slain” (Revelation 5:6). Both see that the song's heart is not delight in death but thanks for rescue. These notes do not choose between them.
passages.asks: The enemy said ‘I will’ six times; God simply breathed. Ask what loud threats in your life seem larger than God right now. And ask what it would mean to sing, as Israel did, before the whole road is behind you.

passages.t: ‘You will lead the people You have redeemed’
passages.happening:
“With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed; with Your strength You will guide them to Your holy dwelling” (verse 13).

“The nations will hear and tremble” (verse 14). Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan will be dismayed, “until Your people pass by, O LORD, until the people You have bought pass by” (verse 16).

“You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance” (verse 17). “The LORD will reign forever and ever!” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Now the song turns from the past to the future. God has rescued; he will also lead. The word ‘loving devotion’ is chesed, God's loyal covenant love, which goes beyond what is owed.

The peoples named, Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, are the peoples Israel would meet on the road to the land.

‘Plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance’ looks ahead to a place where God will dwell among his people. Some read it as the temple hill in Jerusalem, and take that as a sign the song was written later. Others read it as the land of Canaan as a whole, God's own dwelling place.

And the song ends with the great confession: ‘The LORD will reign forever and ever’. Pharaoh's reign is over. God's has no end. The goal of the exodus is not only freedom. It is a people living under God as their King, in his presence.
passages.later:
The psalms often praise God as king in the same words: “The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations” (Psalm 146:10).

Revelation's song of Moses and the Lamb ends, “Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations!” (Revelation 15:3).
passages.asks: The song moves from what God has done to what God will do. Ask what God has already done in your life that gives you courage for what is ahead. And ask what it would mean for you to live, today, as someone whose King reigns forever.

passages.happening:
“For when Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought the waters of the sea back over them. But the Israelites walked through the sea on dry ground” (verse 19).

“Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing” (verse 20).

“And Miriam sang back to them: ‘Sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea’” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Victory songs were known in the ancient world. In Israel women often led the celebration with hand drums and dancing. Jephthah's daughter came out this way to meet her father (Judges 11:34), and the women sang of Saul and David the same way (1 Samuel 18:6-7).

Miriam sings ‘back to them’, call and answer, the women replying with the refrain.

She is called ‘the prophetess’. She is the first woman given that title in the Bible. It shows that she held a recognized place of leadership beside her brothers. This is also the first time she is named. She is most likely the sister who watched over the baby Moses in the reeds (2:4).
passages.later:
The prophet Micah names Miriam with her brothers as God's gift to Israel: “I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam” (Micah 6:4).

When the women of Israel later went out to meet Saul, they came “with singing and dancing, with joyful songs, and with tambourines and other instruments” (1 Samuel 18:6).
passages.asks: Miriam took up a tambourine and led the women in praise. Ask whether you let yourself rejoice in what God has done, with your whole self. And ask whose voice in your church, perhaps an overlooked one, God may be using to lead others in praise.

passages.happening:
“Then Moses led Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the Desert of Shur. For three days they walked in the desert without finding water” (verse 22).

At Marah the water is bitter, “That is why it was named Marah” (verse 23). “So the people grumbled against Moses, saying, ‘What are we to drink?’” (verse 24).

“And Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log. And when he cast it into the waters, they were sweetened” (verse 25). There God tests them, saying, “If you will listen carefully to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in His eyes” and keep his commands, “then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians. For I am the LORD who heals you” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Three days after the song, the people who sang are grumbling. The chapter holds both sides of the wilderness years together: the glory of God's rescue, and how quickly trust can fade. Praise can be real and still short-lived.

The Desert of Shur lay in the northwest of the Sinai Peninsula, east of Egypt's border. Marah means ‘bitter’. Marah and Elim have not been located with certainty. Bitter springs are common in that region, and so are oases with palms and several springs, so the story fits the land even if the exact places are unknown.

Marah begins a series of testing stories: water here, manna in chapter 16, water from the rock in chapter 17. In these God trains a freed people to depend on him before he gives them his law at Sinai.

‘The LORD who heals you.’ The God who struck Egypt with disease is the God who heals his people. Some Christians have read the log thrown into the water as a picture of the cross. That is a later devotional reading; neither the text nor the New Testament says so.

A word of care. This promise does not mean that illness is a punishment, or that anyone who is sick has failed to listen to God. No one should be told that their illness or disability is a punishment. The promise is about God's care for his people, not a guarantee that faithful people will never be ill.
passages.later:
Moses later explains why God led them through the desert: “so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart” (Deuteronomy 8:2).

The psalm praises the God “who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases” (Psalm 103:3). In the Gospels Jesus heals the sick and announces the kingdom of God; the God who heals is at work in him.
passages.asks: Three days after singing, the people were grumbling. Ask how quickly your own praise turns to complaint when life gets hard. And ask what it would look like to cry out to God, as Moses did, instead of grumbling about him.

passages.happening: “Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the waters” (verse 27). After the bitter water of Marah, they rest by springs and shade.
passages.hearers:
After bitter water, a place of plenty. Twelve springs and seventy palm trees: water and shade in the desert.

The numbers may be simply what was there. Many readers have noticed that twelve matches the twelve tribes and seventy the seventy who went down into Egypt (1:5), but the text does not draw the link.

The road with God includes Marahs and Elims. The test comes, and so does rest.
passages.later:
The psalm pictures God's care in the same way: “He leads me beside quiet waters. He restores my soul” (Psalm 23:2-3).

Numbers lists the camps of the road, and Elim is among them: “They set out from Marah and came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and they camped there” (Numbers 33:9).
passages.asks: After the bitter water came twelve springs and seventy palms. Ask whether you are in a Marah or an Elim right now. And ask how you can receive God's rest when it comes, without fearing the next stretch of desert.
